rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ repeats the warning from verse 144, reminding his people that they still have time to fear God and obey him.
rows.anchor: This is the same warning that was sounded in verse 144 earlier. Ṣāliḥ (sws) once again told them that they still have time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ tells them not to follow their leaders, who claim to reform affairs while actually spreading disorder.
rows.anchor: He openly told them to not be lured away by their leaders. Though they claim to be reformers and reforming is their responsibility too, yet they are spreading disorder instead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the universe's peaceful order depends on a single divine intention, and justice on earth requires God's law; alternative laws disrupt justice even if sincerely promoted.
rows.anchor: If any other law is made to govern the earth, then this would end up in disrupting justice in it even though it may have a grand name and is implemented with sincere intentions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word musahhar carries more emphasis and exaggeration than masḥūr.
rows.anchor: carries more emphasis and exaggeration than

rows.speaker: Ṣāliḥ’s nation
rows.claim: They deride Ṣāliḥ's earnest reminders as the obsession of a crazy fanatic who sees their progress as dangerous.
rows.anchor: Ṣāliḥ’s nation rebuked him for his earnest reminders and dubbed him a crazy fanatic who was overreacting to their advancement and development

rows.speaker: Ṣāliḥ’s nation
rows.claim: They object that a messenger should not be an ordinary human like them, asking why God did not send an angel or superhuman instead.
rows.anchor: If God wanted to send a messenger, why would He send a human being like them? Why did He not send an angel or a superhuman for this purpose?

rows.speaker: Ṣāliḥ’s nation
rows.claim: They call him a liar and boaster unless he produces a sign proving divine appointment, saying they will believe his warnings if he does.
rows.anchor: They regard him to be a liar and boaster unless he brings to them a sign of divine appointment. If he brings such a sign, they will believe his warnings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi suggests that the she-camel may have belonged to Ṣāliḥ and says the drinking place was shared by everyone.
rows.anchor: The she-camel mentioned may have belonged to him. It seems evident from these verses that the place of drinking water was the same for everyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The allotted turns at the shared water source were a severe test exposing the people's audacity; harming the camel despite warning would show they would attack Ṣāliḥ too.
rows.anchor: By apportioning time, Ṣāliḥ made this means of severe trial so that the foolhardiness of his nation is fully exposed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation whose rebellion against its messenger reaches this point becomes deserving of punishment under God's established practice.
rows.anchor: it becomes worthy of punishment in accordance with God’s established practice in this matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although one person hamstrung the camel, the Qur’an attributes the crime to the whole nation because the others accepted it and did not object; so punishment engulfed them all.
rows.anchor: Though one person committed his crime but the Qur’ān has ascribed it to the whole nation. The reason for this is that if others agree to such a heinous prank and do not raise their voice against it, it means that they too are involved in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about being left to regret signifies the punishment that followed the camel's slaughter.
rows.anchor: The words “so, they were left to regret” signify the punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Qur’anic passages indicate that after killing the camel the people received three days to recognize their error and repent, but did not use the respite.
rows.anchor: they were given three more days to realize their blunder and repent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These closing refrain verses have appeared before, and their occasion and wording are clear in this context.
rows.anchor: These are the repetitive verses which have been mentioned earlier as well and their occasion and text is fully evident here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section VII shifts from Hūd's and Ṣāliḥ's warnings against excessive construction to Lot's warning against a shameful vice.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws), on the other hand, warned them on a shameful vice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Indifference to God and the Hereafter generates evils that spread through human life, with each nation's circumstances and temperament shaping its most visible disorder.
rows.anchor: evils always come into being because of indifference to God and the Hereafter. For this reason, their disorder spreads in every sphere of human life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot warned his people of the grave consequences of their vice, but they ignored him and met the fate he had warned them about; the repeated ending shows that all the anecdotes serve the same purpose.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws) warned his nation of its grave consequences but it did not pay heed and ultimately met the fate he warned them of. This anecdote also ends on the repetitive verses.

words: إِذْ قَالَ لَهُمْ أَخُوهُمْ لُوطٌ أَلَا تَتَّقُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening messenger appeal and command to fear God and obey Lot recur in earlier anecdotes and were explained there.
rows.anchor: These verses occur in the previous anecdotes also. They have been explained there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Homosexuality had become fashionable among Lot's people; when a nation embraces it, Islahi calls it filth from which God cleanses the earth.
rows.anchor: homosexuality had become fashion among them. When this happens in a nation, it becomes a pile of filth. God cleanses his earth from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning men after 'among people of the world' highlights their blindness: women were present and plainly visible, yet they pursued men; Islahi connects this to al-Naml 27:54.
rows.anchor: The word “men” after “among people of the world” point to the utter blindness of his nation.

words: وَتَذَرُونَ مَا خَلَقَ لَكُم رَّبُّكُم مِّنْ أَزْوَٰجِكُم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving the wives God created explains their blindness and the consequence of this perversion: attraction to women disappears.
rows.anchor: The words “and leave the wives which your Lord has created for you?” is an explanation of this blindness and the essential consequence of this vulgar tendency.

words: وَتَذَرُونَ مَا خَلَقَ لَكُم رَّبُّكُم مِّنْ أَزْوَٰجِكُم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such people mock the family and turn society into a herd governed by unnatural desires.
rows.anchor: Such people make a complete mockery of the institution of family and the society becomes a herd of animals driven by unnatural desires.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them people who cross limits conveys yearning and sorrow because their wrongdoing exceeds the limits of human nature.
rows.anchor: The words “in fact, you are a people who have crossed the limits” express yearning and sorrow.

words: قَالُوا لَئِن لَّمْ تَنتَهِ يَٰلُوطُ لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْمُخْرَجِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their wording makes the threat a decisive warning, not an empty threat; although they had threatened earlier, this time they meant to carry it out.
rows.anchor: The style of this threat clearly shows that it was not merely a threat: it was a decisive warning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word qālīn means intense hate and malice.
rows.anchor: The word )ﻗ means “intense hate and malice.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot answers their decisive threat emphatically: their hatred and threats will neither make him yield nor soften his condemnation of their vulgarity.
rows.anchor: their threats can neither stop him nor soften him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural 'among those who hate' stresses that all upright people reject the act; Lot belongs among them and cannot be their companion in it.
rows.anchor: stress has been added to his response. The implication is that it is not merely he who is averse to it;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A governing noun is omitted in the expression mimmā according to a common linguistic principle, so the intended expression is mā.
rows.anchor: a governing noun is suppressed in accordance with a common linguistic principle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot judges that the decisive moment has arrived: expulsion would mean that, by God's established practice, punishment must come, so he prays for deliverance.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws) assessed that the decisive moment had arrived; if these people have decided to expel him from the land, then in accordance with the established practice of God a torment will necessarily visit them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term 'family' includes Lot's followers, so any members of his people who believed in him are included in the prayer.
rows.anchor: also includes followers. Hence, if some people from among his nation professed faith in him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The details of Lot's people's punishment were explained earlier in Sūrah al-Ḥijr.
rows.anchor: After that, the torment descended on the nation of Lot (sws), the details of which have already been explained in Sūrah al-Ḥijr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The old woman is Lot's wife; her sympathies remained with her people, so she was punished despite belonging to Lot's family.
rows.anchor: refers to his wife. All her sympathies were with her nation. Thus in spite of belonging to Lot’s family she was punished.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the phrase 'old woman' is used disparagingly for Lot's wife.
rows.anchor: This word has been used here for her disparagingly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning about the evil rain is directed at Quraysh: people who ignore a messenger's warnings eventually face God's torment.
rows.anchor: The words “so, what evil was the rain that was unleashed on them who had been warned of their fate” are meant to warn the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These closing refrain verses have already been explained.
rows.anchor: These repetitive verses at the end have already been explained.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the anecdotes conclude with Shuʿayb, the historical sequence reaches Moses; his story is omitted because it was detailed earlier, and the discourse returns to its main theme.
rows.anchor: These anecdotes ended on the account of Shu‘ayb (sws) and his people. After this, the era of Moses (sws) begins as per the historical sequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage returns to the claim that the Qur’an was sent by God, not inspired by a devil or composed as poetry.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has been sent down by God; it is not inspired by some devil nor is it poetry.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier scriptures predicted the Qur’an, and Israelite scholars know these prophecies.
rows.anchor: Previous scriptures have predicted it and the scholars of the Israelites are aware of these prophesies.

words: فَإِنْ عَصَوْكَ فَقُلْ إِنِّي بَرِيءٌ مِّمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the deniers reject the message, the Prophet should not let them distract him; he should focus on the believers as the deniers approach their fate.
rows.anchor: If these unfortunate people deny it, the Prophet (sws) should not pay heed to them. Instead he should focus all his attention on the believers.
